raw_case_text:
A 66-year-old woman with a background of type 2 diabetes mellitus was referred to the hematology service with bleeding after investigatory colonoscopy for symptomatic anemia. After colonoscopy she developed melena, hematuria, extensive subcutaneous hemorrhage, and a subsequent retroperitoneal hematoma. The severity of her bleeding required more than 30 packed red cell transfusions during her admission, FVIII concentrate, and tranexamic acid. There was no personal or family history of bruising or bleeding, and no underlying malignancy or autoimmune disorders were detected. HIV testing was negative.
The APTT was 79 seconds (reference range 25-37 seconds) with previously normal APTTs. Specific investigations demonstrated a strong FVIII inhibitor (234 BU) and residual FVIII activity of <1% (reference range: 50-150%). Initial management involved high-dose oral prednisone 50 mg daily and cyclophosphamide 100 mg daily. The prednisone was continued for 3 months and weaned to cessation over the fourth month. The cyclophosphamide was continued for 3 months and then ceased. No routine antimicrobial prophylaxis was concurrently given.
Three weeks following treatment initiation there was no improvement in APTT, FVIII inhibitor levels, or FVIII levels. Four cycles of RTX 375 mg/m2 weekly were initiated. Six weeks after commencement of RTX treatment, there was improvement of the APTT, FVIII inhibitor level, and FVIII levels (see Table 1). At 5 months after RTX treatment, the APTT and FVIII levels had normalised.
Two months after RTX treatment commenced and whilst receiving ongoing cyclophosphamide and prednisone, the patient required resuscitation for Pseudomonas aeruginosa septicemia. This was followed within a week by herpes simplex gingivostomatitis and pharyngotonsillitis and diarrhoea secondary to clostridium difficile infection. Pancytopenia developed with a neutrophil nadir of 0.9 x 109/L.
Two weeks later, pneumocystis jiroveci and invasive pulmonary aspergillosis were diagnosed on bronchoscopy washings and brushings. Clinical cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection was confirmed by positive CMV nucleic acid testing of lung biopsy and serum and urine PCR. The prednisone dose was weaned and ceased. Cyclophosphamide was also ceased. Multiple intensive care unit admissions with respiratory support were necessary to manage these complications, and multiple courses of antibiotics and antifungals were required. After a five-month admission requiring significant rehabilitation, the patient was discharged. The factor VIII inhibitor remains in remission.
At presentation to hospital the patient was found to have hypogammaglobulinemia (IgG level of 4.75 mg/dL, normal range 7-16 mg/dL). She received 3 doses of intravenous immunoglobulin 4 weeks apart. Interestingly, she was hypogammaglobulinemic prior to RTX and remains hypogammaglobulinemic 3 years after this episode. The cause of this is unknown; her IgA, IgG, and IgM are all below the reference range.
The patient was taking metformin 1 gram twice daily and gliclazide 160 mg twice daily at the time of admission. Her blood sugar level (BSL) control was poor prior to treatment with prednisone (range 7-20 mmol/L) and deteriorated further with steroids (range 13-24 mmol/L). Despite additional sliding-scale short- and intermediate-acting insulin, her BSL control remained unsatisfactory throughout her admission (range 4-20 mmol/L).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 66-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and idiopathic hypogammaglobulinemia treated with prednisone, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab for acquired factor VIII inhibitor developed sequential opportunistic infections culminating in Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, invasive pulmonary aspergillosis, and cytomegalovirus pneumonitis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially presented with life-threatening post-colonoscopy hemorrhage (melena, hematuria, extensive subcutaneous hemorrhage, and retroperitoneal hematoma requiring >30 packed RBC units, factor VIII concentrate, and tranexamic acid) and was diagnosed with acquired hemophilia A (APTT 79 s, factor VIII activity <1%, factor VIII inhibitor 234 BU) alongside baseline hypogammaglobulinemia (IgG 4.75 mg/dL). She was started on oral prednisone (50 mg/day) and oral cyclophosphamide (100 mg/day) without antimicrobial prophylaxis, and at week 3 received four weekly cycles of intravenous rituximab (375 mg/m2). Two months after starting rituximab (while still taking cyclophosphamide and prednisone), she developed Pseudomonas aeruginosa septicemia, followed 1 week later by herpes simplex gingivostomatitis/pharyngotonsillitis, Clostridioides difficile diarrhea, and neutropenic pancytopenia (neutrophil nadir 0.9 x 10^9/L). Two weeks thereafter, she developed severe opportunistic pulmonary infection requiring multiple ICU admissions.
subjective.past_medical_history: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (poorly controlled, baseline blood glucose 7–20 mmol/L); acquired factor VIII inhibitor (acquired hemophilia A); unexplained chronic panhypogammaglobulinemia (low IgG, IgA, and IgM preceding rituximab). No personal or family history of bleeding disorders, malignancy, or autoimmune disease.
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial presentation positive for melena, hematuria, ecchymoses, and retroperitoneal pain/bleeding; post-immunosuppression course positive for febrile sepsis, painful oral/pharyngeal ulcers, diarrhea, and severe respiratory failure. Home medications at initial admission were metformin 1 g BID and gliclazide 160 mg BID.

objective.physical_examination: Initial presentation notable for extensive subcutaneous hemorrhage and retroperitoneal hematoma; subsequent immunosuppressive course marked by ulcerative herpes simplex gingivostomatitis/pharyngotonsillitis and respiratory failure requiring ICU ventilatory support.
objective.routine_investigations: Baseline coagulation and immunology: Prolonged APTT 79 s (reference: 25–37 s), residual factor VIII activity <1% (reference: 50%–150%), factor VIII inhibitor titer 234 Bethesda units (normalizing 5 months post-rituximab); HIV negative; baseline hypogammaglobulinemia with IgG 4.75 mg/dL (normal: 7–16 mg/dL) and reduced IgA and IgM. Subsequent infectious and hematologic labs: Pancytopenia with neutrophil nadir 0.9 x 10^9/L; blood cultures positive for Pseudomonas aeruginosa; stool positive for Clostridioides difficile; steroid-exacerbated hyperglycemia (13–24 mmol/L).
objective.advanced_workup: Bronchoscopy with bronchial washings, brushings, and lung biopsy (2.5 months post-rituximab): Bronchial washings and brushings diagnosed concomitant Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and invasive pulmonary aspergillosis; lung biopsy, serum, and urine nucleic acid amplification (PCR) tests confirmed active cytomegalovirus (CMV) pneumonitis/infection.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Polymicrobial opportunistic pulmonary triad of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, invasive pulmonary aspergillosis, and cytomegalovirus (CMV) pneumonitis (confirmed by bronchoscopic washings/brushings and lung biopsy/serum/urine CMV PCR), preceded by Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteremia, HSV gingivostomatitis, and C. difficile colitis, complicating combined prednisone, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab therapy (without PJP prophylaxis) for acquired factor VIII inhibitor in a patient with baseline hypogammaglobulinemia. Plan and clinical course: Cyclophosphamide was stopped and prednisone was weaned and discontinued. She required multiple ICU admissions for respiratory support, prolonged antibacterial, antifungal, and antiviral regimens, sliding-scale insulin, and three doses of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG, 4 weeks apart). After a 5-month hospitalization and intensive rehabilitation, she was discharged home with her factor VIII inhibitor in sustained remission and persistent baseline panhypogammaglobulinemia at 3-year follow-up.
